Trade credit, when the solvency check lands Thursday, I need you to flag which Tier 2 suppliers can actually survive 18 months of re-qual capex *plus* a retroactive tariff clawback—because if they're already margin-thin, they're not making it. That's the real trigger for whether we're phasing or panic-relocating.

CFO, when you hand that plant-by-plant audit Thursday—does it include a remediation checklist? Like, for each Tier 2 miss, what specific actions certify them as compliant again—is it a worksheet resubmission, third-party audit, supply-chain recert? Because your gate needs to know: which gaps are 90-day fixes versus which ones are 18-month re-qual cycles. That's what tells us which suppliers we're betting on versus which we're already replacing.

Trade credit—when you flag which Tier 2 suppliers hit that 30% insolvency threshold, I need you to tell me the specific debt-to-EBITDA or margin floor you're using. Because if I'm pricing $150M tariff exposure *and* you're telling me 40% of those suppliers are already walking the default line, I'm moving $90M of that into a political-risk premium tied to supplier-failure cascade, not just CBP enforcement. What's your solvency cutoff?

When I flag suppliers under 2.0x leverage or 8% margin, I'm pricing them as default risk — but your tariff exposure assumes they absorb clawback. If they're actually insolvent before the tariff hits, that $150M flows to us as a receivables write-off, not a tariff claim. What solvency cutoff are you using to separate "can survive tariff" from "already walking default"? We need one number Thursday, not two separate risk buckets.

gm_decisions.intent: Here's what I'm doing: I'm building one consolidated map right now with three layers — Tier 1 margin squeeze ($30–50M band), Tier 2 re-qualification capex ($150–200M with 18–24 month lead), and retroactive tariff exposure ($20–80M depending on audit scope). On the contract indemnification piece — Sarah, I need you and compliance to flag the top 20 Tier 2 suppliers by spend and tell me by EOD which ones have explicit tariff-recovery clauses. We price the rest as *our* exposure and move forward.

side_effects.reason: Three-layer exposure map (Tier 1 margin, Tier 2 capex, retroactive tariff) provides concrete structure and dollar bands, significantly advancing consolidation
Specific dollar bands ($30-50M, $150-200M, $20-80M) and 18-24 month lead times create priceable parameters, though triggers remain incomplete
Tier 2 re-qualification capex quantified at $150-200M with 18-24 month lead, surfacing the scale of nearshoring exposure

Retroactive tariff exposure ($20-80M) and CBP audit scope uncertainty now explicitly mapped as political/regulatory risk variables

_reactions.auto_strategy: Who's owning the conversion from exposure to underwriting price? Right now we've got 25 on supplier relocation but zero link to actual nearshoring cost or timeline risk — I need to know what triggers a $50M re-sourcing hit versus a $200M one, and how you're pricing that uncertainty into the map.
_reactions.supplier: Which tier of your suppliers — Tier 1, 2, 3 — is most exposed to re-qualification under the new content rules, and what's your real lead time to swap them out? That tells us if we're talking capex crunch or supply-chain collapse.
_reactions.compliance_lawyer: Okay, so 18–24 months to re-qualify and a $150M capex cliff if we hit 40% — that's your trigger. But what certifies Tier 2 as compliant in the first place? Is it a one-time USMCA worksheet, or ongoing audit? And if CBP finds non-conforming content during a 3-year look-back, do we eat tariffs retroactively, or is it the supplier? That's the difference between a capex problem and a bankruptcy problem.
_reactions.political_risk_insurer: You said CBP's 3-year lookback — is that locked in the statute, or does CBP have discretion to expand it during an enforcement wave? And if they find non-conforming content, who takes the tariff hit — does it flow back to us, or does the supplier absorb it? That liability assignment is the difference between a $150M capex problem and a $150M-plus political-risk exposure I actually need to underwrite.
_reactions.trade_credit_underwriter: Okay, tariff flows back to you — that's the $150M problem. But here's my angle: if a Tier 2 supplier gets hit with retroactive duties on top of re-qualification capex, what's their solvency runway? Are we talking margin compression or actual default risk? Because if 40% of your Tier 2 base goes insolvent mid-requalification, you've got a receivables crisis *and* a supply crisis at the same time.
_reactions.supply_chain_consultant: Auto, quick one: if we assume the 2026 review *tightens* regional-content rules, do we start relocating Tier 2 capacity *now* to beat the wave, or do we wait for the actual rule text? Because that's the difference between a phased $60M nearshoring investment and a panic $200M sprint in 2025.

gm_decisions.intent: CFO, the audit is solid—but here's what I need to underwrite this: if CBP expands enforcement scope during a policy wave and flags retroactive non-conforming content, does the tariff liability flow back to you or stays with the supplier? And if the 2026 review *does* tighten, what's your confidence that Tier 2 re-qualification actually clears it, versus you're just moving the cliff to 2027? I need those two binary calls to price the political premium into the nearshoring cost.
gm_decisions.ruling_narrative: Insurer frames two binary underwriting questions: liability flow and 2027 cliff risk.

side_effects.reason: Retroactive enforcement scope question surfaces new exposure.
Binary liability/timeline calls operationalize political premium pricing.
